analysis.one_liner: Ties federal airport funding to a $15 minimum wage and benefits for airport service workers.
analysis.headline: The bill, which would require airports to certify that security, cleaning, food service, and other workers earn at least $15 an hour with benefits before receiving federal airport grants, was introduced with 15 Senate sponsors and never received a committee hearing or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have required airports of all hub sizes to certify that their service workers — security officers, cleaners, baggage handlers, food and retail workers, and similar jobs — are paid at least $15 an hour plus fringe benefits, or whatever is higher among the federal Service Contract Act prevailing wage, the federal contractor minimum wage, and the local minimum wage. Airports that failed to certify would lose access to federal airport development grants, including funds already appropriated under the bipartisan infrastructure law. It also created annual compliance reporting by the companies that actually employ the workers.
analysis.who_benefits: Airport service workers at small, medium, and large hub airports nationwide: security officers, cleaning staff, baggage and ramp handlers, ticketing agents, food service and retail workers, cabin cleaners, and hotel and lounge staff on airport property. The bill's wage floor is set at the highest of $15 per hour, the Service Contract Act prevailing wage for their job and locality, the federal contractor minimum wage, or the state or local minimum wage — so in high-wage cities it would raise pay above $15. It also covers fringe benefits such as health coverage, and it covers workers no matter what subcontracting arrangement their employer claims, closing a common loophole. The bill's own findings argue stable, better-paid airport workforces improve safety, security, and public health.

how_it_helps.text: Sets a pay floor for covered airport service workers at the highest of $15 per hour, the Service Contract Act prevailing wage for their locality and job class, the federal contractor minimum wage, or the applicable state or local minimum wage.
Requires a matching floor on fringe benefits, at the higher of the Service Contract Act minimum for the locality or any state or local requirement.

Conditions federal airport development grants, passenger facility charge authority, and discretionary grants on the airport certifying compliance, and restricts airport infrastructure and terminal funds from the 2021 infrastructure law to compliant airports.
Counts workers as covered regardless of any alleged contractual relationship with a contractor or subcontractor, so employers cannot dodge the standard through subcontracting chains.
Preserves any state or local law that requires higher wages or better benefits, so the federal standard is a floor, not a ceiling.

analysis.who_pays: The airports and the companies that employ airport service workers — airlines, airline service contractors, concessionaires, catering firms, and airport-terminal hotels — would bear higher payroll and benefits costs. Airport operators would also take on annual certification and compliance-reporting duties, and an airport that did not comply would lose access to federal airport development grants, including infrastructure-law airport grants. Some of the cost could ultimately surface in concession prices or airfares.

drawbacks.text: The mandate raises labor costs for airports, airlines, and service contractors, and some of that cost could be passed on to travelers through higher concession prices, parking, or airfares.

Tying federal airport development grants to labor certification could hold up infrastructure projects at airports that cannot immediately certify compliance, trading construction timelines for wage standards.

The bill relies on annual self-certification by employers and airport sponsors rather than an audit or penalty regime spelled out in the bill, so enforcement would depend heavily on the Secretary of Transportation's implementation.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is higher pay and benefits for a large, largely low-wage workforce — often employed through subcontractors specifically to keep wages down — against higher operating costs for airports and their contractors and a modest risk of higher prices for travelers. The compliance mechanism (annual certifications with federal grant money as leverage) is a standard and reasonably strong design. On balance the benefits go directly to working people, and the costs fall on a concentrated set of employers; the main honest caveat is enforcement, which rests on certifications rather than built-in audits.

outcome.mechanism: The Senate bill was introduced in June 2022 and referred to the Commerce, Science, and Transportation Committee, which never acted on it, and the Congress ended in January 2023 with no hearing, no committee vote, and no floor vote in either chamber.

narrative.text: Sen. Edward Markey introduced the bill on June 16, 2022, joined by 10 original co-sponsors including Sens. Schumer, Sanders, Warren, Booker, and Blumenthal.
Fifteen senators sponsored the bill in total: 14 of the Senate's 48 Democrats plus Independent Sen. Sanders; no Republican sponsored it.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Senate Committee on Commerce, Science, and Transportation on the day it was introduced, and that is the last action listed in its record.
No further action — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor vote in the Senate, and no House companion action — appears before the 117th Congress ended on January 3, 2023.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Airport operators, airlines, and the contractors that employ airport service workers are better off, since they never faced the $15 wage-and-benefits mandate or the compliance costs tied to federal airport grants. No version of the bill advanced in the House.

sides.party_line_note: All 15 sponsors were Democrats or the Independent Sen. Sanders (14 of 48 Senate Democrats, 1 of 2 Independents), with no Republican support in the record; the bill never reached a vote, so no roll-call split exists.

industries.note: They employ most covered service workers — baggage and ramp handling, cleaning, security, catering — frequently through subcontracting, and the bill would have raised their wage and benefits costs while closing the subcontracting loophole. Their savings from low wages are the workers' lost income.

Airports would have gained federal grant money as before but only by certifying worker wages and running annual compliance reports; non-compliance would cost them airport development and terminal funding. The burden falls on them, while the wage standard benefits the workers on their property.

industries.industry: Airport concession, food service, and catering firms
industries.note: Concessionaires, food and beverage service, duty-free and lounge operators, and airline caterers are explicitly covered and would have faced the same wage and benefits floor.

Not an industry but the bill's direct beneficiaries: security, cleaning, ground handling, concessions, and hotel workers on airport property would have gained a wage and benefits floor regardless of which contractor signs their paycheck.
